property_summary: For every call, the correct contract returns the stored pause flag (_paused) via paused() (i.e., paused() == false immediately after initialization or when not paused), whereas the mutant returns the negation and thus for some inputs (e.g., immediately after initialize) paused() differs.

For every input, the reference contract's paused() accurately reflects the internal _paused state (returns true if paused, false if not); the mutant that always returns false violates this because there exist inputs where the contract is paused but paused() would incorrectly return false.

For any caller with LRT_MANAGER role, calling pause() changes c.paused() from false to true (the reference reports paused()==true after pause); the mutant that always returns false breaks this since after pause() it still returns false for some inputs (a manager caller).

For any caller address, after calling pause() as an account that has the LRT_MANAGER role the reference contract's paused() returns true, whereas the mutant that always returns false will return false for some such caller addresses (i.e. when pause() succeeds).

For every address caller, calling pause() then reading paused() returns true on the correct contract, but the mutant that always returns false will return false for some caller (i.e., there exists a caller for which paused() ≠ true after pause()); the test fuzzes the caller address to find such a case.

For every caller who is an admin (can call updateLRTConfig) the reference contract preserves the paused() status: immediately after calling pause() (via an allowed manager) a subsequent call to paused() returns true; the mutant that always returns false violates this for those inputs.

For any nonzero admin caller and any input address, calling updateLRTConfig on the correct contract reverts when passed the zero address (preserving that lrtConfig cannot be set to address(0)), whereas the mutant removes that check and accepts address(0) — so the property is that updateLRTConfig(address(0)) must revert for the reference but the mutant will succeed for some admin caller and input.

For any caller that has the LRT admin role, calling updateLRTConfig with address(0) must revert on the reference (it forbids zero address) but the mutant accepts and sets lrtConfig to address(0), so there exists an admin caller for which updateLRTConfig(address(0)) succeeds on the mutant but not on the reference.

For every admin caller and every lrtConfigAddr, the reference contract reverts when attempting to set lrtConfig to address(0) (enforcing non-zero), so calling updateLRTConfig with a fuzzed caller that is NOT the default admin must always revert due to onlyLRTAdmin; the mutant that allows address(0) will allow a non-admin (fuzzed) address to succeed in setting lrtConfig to address(0) only if access-control check is lost via setting lrtConfig to zero previously — therefore there exists a sequence where a fuzzed admin first sets lrtConfig to a benign contract, then a second fuzzed admin (not role holder) attempts to set lrtConfig to address(0): the reference prevents setting lrtConfig to zero (reverts) while the mutant allows it — the property asserts that for any fuzzed caller and an arbitrary helper admin contract deployed, calling updateLRTConfig(address(0)) by a non-admin always reverts on the reference (i.e., the call does not succeed), whereas the mutant will sometimes allow the call to succeed and set lrtConfig to zero; we test that calling updateLRTConfig with the fuzzed caller does not succeed (reference invariant).

For any caller, calling updateLRTConfig with an arbitrary address must either revert due to access control (caller not LRT admin) or, if the caller is the LRT admin, the reference contract always rejects setting lrtConfig to address(0) (reverts); the mutant accepts address(0) and thus there exists an input (an admin caller attempting to set address(0)) where mutant succeeds but the reference reverts.

For every caller, calling updateLRTConfig with the zero address must revert (reference enforces non-zero), whereas the mutant allows updateLRTConfig(address(0)) to succeed for some caller — so the property: updateLRTConfig(address(0)) never succeeds on the reference (always reverts).

For any caller address, calling updateLRTConfig on the correct contract succeeds iff the caller has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00); the mutant inverts this check and will revert for admin callers, so there exist admin addresses for which the mutant rejects updateLRTConfig while the reference accepts it.

For all addresses adminAddr, calling updateLRTConfig(adminAddr) should succeed when msg.sender has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in the correct contract; the mutant inverts the admin check and will revert for such admin callers, so there exist inputs (an admin caller) that make the mutant revert while the reference accepts.

For any caller address that is an admin according to lrtConfig.hasRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, caller), the reference contract allows updateLRTConfig(callee) to succeed; the mutant reverts for such admin callers (inverts the check), so there exists an admin caller input where the mutant rejects updateLRTConfig while the reference accepts it.

For any caller address that is the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE per lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(...) should succeed on the reference C; the mutant inverts the admin check and will revert for such admin callers, so there exist inputs (an admin caller) where the mutant rejects updateLRTConfig while the reference accepts it.

For any caller address that has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE according to the configured lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(...) should succeed (reference permits admins to call it); the mutant inverts the check and will revert when the caller IS an admin, so there exist admin callers for which the mutant reverts while the reference succeeds.

After initialize(...) completes, maxNodeDelegatorCount is non-zero for all valid lrtConfig addresses in the reference contract (initialized to 10) but the mutant sets it to 0, so the invariant 'c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 0 after initialize' holds for all inputs on reference and is violated by the mutant for some input (any valid lrtConfig address).

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a nonzero positive value (10) after initialization; the mutant that sets it to 0 violates this by producing maxNodeDelegatorCount == 0 for some valid input.

For every nonzero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the correct contract ensures maxNodeDelegatorCount > nodeDelegatorQueue.length after initialization (so there is room for at least one node delegator), while the mutant that sets maxNodeDelegatorCount = 0 can violate this for some inputs by making maxNodeDelegatorCount == 0 (not greater than queue length).

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a positive constant (10) whereas the mutant may set it to 0; therefore after initialize(address) completes on the reference maxNodeDelegatorCount >= 1, but the mutant can produce maxNodeDelegatorCount == 0 for some valid input.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a positive value (>=1) so that addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue will accept at least one element when queue is empty; the mutant initializes maxNodeDelegatorCount to 0 and therefore for some valid lrtConfig addresses the call to addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue with a single non-zero address will revert (MaximumNodeDelegatorCountReached), violating the rule.

For every nonzero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10; the mutant sets it to 100, so there exists inputs where c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 10 (mutant breaks the rule).

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the correct contract C always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialization; the mutant sets it to 100 for some inputs, so the invariant maxNodeDelegatorCount == 10 is violated by the mutant.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the correct contract C always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialize returns; the mutant sets it to 100 for some inputs, so asserting that c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 distinguishes them.

For every non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize(...), the reference C sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 and thus c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 always holds; the mutant sets it to 100 for some valid lrtConfig addresses, so asserting the getter equals 10 will fail on the mutant for some fuzzed addresses.

For any address passed to initialize that is the zero address the call reverts; for any non-zero address initialize succeeds and sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a small value <= 10 in the reference but the mutant sets it to 100 — so the universal property: if initialize succeeds then c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() <= 10 (reference satisfies for all admissible inputs, mutant violates for some).

For any nonzero lrtConfig address, calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) on the correct contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 (the initializer's assignment); the mutant that omits setting _initialized = 1 can leave initialize ineffective under reentrancy/initialization detection differences and therefore can result in maxNodeDelegatorCount not being 10 for some inputs.

For any nonzero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialize(...) returns; the mutant (which omits setting _initialized = 1 in the initializer modifier) can allow initialize to be called in a way that leaves maxNodeDelegatorCount at 0 for some fuzzed lrtConfig address scenario, so the property is violated by the mutant for some input.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize(...), the reference contract C always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialize returns; the mutant that omits setting _initialized = 1 in the initializer modifier can allow initialize to be ineffective in some scenarios so maxNodeDelegatorCount remains 0 for some fuzzed lrtConfig addresses.

For any nonzero lrtConfig address input, calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) on the correct contract always results in maxNodeDelegatorCount == 10 after the call; the mutant (which omits setting _initialized = 1 in the initializer modifier) can leave initialization ineffective for some lrtConfigAddr values so maxNodeDelegatorCount != 10.

For every non-zero lrtConfig address input, calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) on the correct contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10; the mutant (which omits setting _initialized = 1 in the initializer modifier) can leave initialization ineffective for some lrtConfig addresses so maxNodeDelegatorCount != 10.
